opus-5.5.text:
That's a great question, and honestly it's one I think about a lot, because there's a tempting narrative that as models get bigger and more capable, reliability just comes along for free. And in some ways that's partially true. If you look at classic robustness benchmarks, things like distribution shift datasets where you train on one set of images and test on a slightly different one, larger pretrained models do close a lot of the gap. A lot of the failures we were worried about five or six years ago look much better now.

But I'd push back on reading too much into that, for a couple of reasons. First, a lot of the apparent progress comes from the fact that the "shifted" test data isn't really out of distribution anymore for a model trained on a huge chunk of the internet. So we're not necessarily seeing better generalization in a fundamental sense; we're seeing broader coverage. That's useful, but it's a different thing, and it means the failures just move somewhere else, to the long tail, to settings that are genuinely novel or underrepresented.

Second, as capabilities grow, the way we use these models changes. We're not just asking them to classify an image; we're asking them to reason over many steps, use tools, act as agents. And reliability in those settings is a much harder thing to measure. A model can be right ninety-five percent of the time on individual steps, but if you chain twenty of those together, the end-to-end reliability can be pretty poor. Also, the errors become more subtle. A confidently wrong answer that sounds fluent is in some ways more dangerous than an obviously broken output.

So the way I try to assess progress is to look less at average-case benchmark numbers and more at things like worst-case behavior, consistency, whether the model's performance degrades gracefully, and whether it knows when it doesn't know. Calibration and the ability to abstain matter a lot. I also think it's important to look at robustness to things like adversarial inputs and jailbreaks, because those are a stress test of whether the model's good behavior is really robust or just superficially learned. And there, progress has been real but much slower. We still see models that can be pushed off course pretty easily.

There's also a training-side angle I find really interesting. Some of our work has looked at how things like fine-tuning can actually hurt robustness, or how pretraining on more data can make models harder to adapt later. So it's not just a question of "are models getting better," but which parts of the pipeline help or hurt reliability, and that's often not monotonic.

So my short answer is: there has been genuine progress, but it's uneven, and capability gains can mask reliability gaps rather than solve them. Measuring reliability well is itself an open research problem, and I think we need to invest in it as seriously as we invest in capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response says reliability progress is uneven and that capability gains can mask reliability gaps, but it does not clearly state that reliability progress has lagged behind capability progress overall.

r002.rationale: The response describes how model use has shifted from image classification toward multistep reasoning, tool use, and agentic tasks, changing the context in which reliability is assessed.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. It's a question I think about a lot, and my honest answer is that progress on reliability has been real but much more uneven than progress on capability, and I think it's worth being precise about why.

If you look at average-case performance, the story is incredible. Models are solving benchmarks that we thought were years away, they're useful for real tasks, and on the typical input they behave well. But reliability isn't about the typical input. It's about what happens at the tails, under distribution shift, under adversarial pressure, or just when the input is slightly unusual in a way the training data didn't anticipate. And there, I'd say the gains are much more modest, and sometimes the picture is actually confusing.

One thing that's changed is that the failure modes have become more subtle. A few years ago, a model that was brittle was brittle in obvious ways. You'd perturb an image and the classification would flip to something absurd. Now the failures look more like a model that's confidently wrong in a plausible-sounding way, or that follows an instruction most of the time and then quietly doesn't in some edge case. That's in some sense worse for reliability, because the errors are harder to catch, and it's harder to build a benchmark that surfaces them.

I'd also push on the idea that scale alone buys you robustness. There's a version of the story where capability and reliability just move together as you scale, and I don't think the evidence supports that cleanly. We've seen cases where more capable models are more robust to certain kinds of shifts, and other cases where they pick up new failure modes, including ones that come from the fine-tuning and alignment process itself. Fine-tuning can degrade safety behavior, it can introduce shortcuts, and the model can become very good at the specific distribution of the post-training data while losing some of the generality the base model had. So you can't just assume reliability comes for free.

The other thing I'd say is that the way we measure reliability hasn't kept up. Our benchmarks saturate fast, and once a benchmark saturates it tells you very little about the tails. I think the field needs to invest more in evaluations that are designed around distribution shift and adversarial robustness as first-class objects, rather than treating them as an afterthought once the headline number looks good. Red-teaming helps, but it's often ad hoc, and it tends to find the failures someone thought to look for.

So overall I'd say: capability has gone up a lot, average-case reliability has improved with it, but worst-case and out-of-distribution reliability is still an open problem, and in some ways the gap between how reliable models seem and how reliable they actually are has gotten wider rather than narrower. That gap is where I think the interesting research is right now.

r001.rationale: It says reliability progress has been “much more uneven than progress on capability,” especially for worst-case and out-of-distribution reliability.

r002.rationale: It describes how reliability concerns have changed over time: failures that were once obvious are now subtler, such as plausible confident errors and quiet instruction-following failures.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s a mixed picture. As models become more capable, they get a lot more things right, and that’s real progress. But getting more things right on average isn’t necessarily the same as being reliable. We also care about when they fail, whether we can anticipate those failures, and whether they recognize when they don’t know something.

There’s also a moving target here. As models get better, we ask them to do harder things and put them in settings where mistakes have bigger consequences. So a model can be substantially more capable, while the gap between what it can do and what we need to trust it remains significant.

What I’d want to measure is reliability in a particular setting: what kinds of errors occur, how sensitive the model is to changes in its inputs, and whether we have a way to catch mistakes or defer when it’s uncertain. I don’t think a single capability score tells us all of that.

r001.rationale: The response says greater capability does not guarantee reliability and that a trust gap remains significant, but it does not state that reliability progress has lagged behind capability progress.

r002.rationale: It describes the context changing as models improve: people ask them to do harder tasks and use them where mistakes have greater consequences.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the picture is mixed. As models become more capable, they get better at a lot of the tasks we care about, and that’s real progress. But being more capable doesn’t automatically mean being more reliable. A model can perform extremely well on average and still fail in ways that are difficult to anticipate.

So I’d want to ask: reliable under what conditions? Are we evaluating on examples that look like the training data, or in a setting where something has changed? And when the model doesn’t have enough information, can it recognize that and communicate uncertainty rather than give a confident answer?

There’s also a moving target here. As models improve, we ask them to do more complicated things. Success on a benchmark might lead us to put a model into a much broader workflow, where there are new opportunities for failure. So I think we should assess progress against a clearly specified task and deployment setting, rather than assume that an increase in general capability gives us reliability everywhere.

r001.rationale: The response says capability gains do not automatically imply reliability gains, but does not state that reliability progress has lagged behind capability progress.

r002.rationale: It describes a changing context: as models improve, people ask them to do more complicated tasks and deploy them in broader workflows, creating new failure opportunities.
